accuracy.evidence: Checked against Common Core RL.1.6 (identify who is telling the story at various points), RL.2.6 (acknowledge differences in the points of view of characters), RL.2.3 (describe how characters respond to major events and challenges) and RL.1.9/RL.2.9 (compare adventures and experiences of characters). First person = narrator uses I/me/we in the narration; third person = he/she/they, matching standard definitions. The traditional-tale details used were checked against common retellings: the wolf huffs and puffs and cannot blow down the brick house; Baby Bear's chair is broken and his porridge eaten all up; the Gingerbread Man runs from everyone, trusts the fox and is eaten; the third pig is safe at the end. Every 'I inside speech marks' line ("I am lost," said the little duck) is correctly classed as third person.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the documented slips named in the adult text: assuming the main character is the teller (step 1 prediction about Jack, the Jack item with 'someone outside the story', challenge 'named'); counting an I inside speech marks (step 2 prediction about the duck, two speech-mark lines with feedback 'The I is inside the speech marks', challenge 'speech'); treating a different feeling as wrong (challenge 'wrong', 'one'); giving the problem instead of the response (step 4 feedback 'That is the problem. Find what Pip did about it', challenge 'problem'); and mixing up facts across two stories (step 5 feedback, challenge 'facts').

lab_distinct.evidence: flagteller works on this topic's own mechanism: pronoun clues outside speech marks decide the narrator, character wants decide reactions to one event, a response is located as one sentence among problem and setting sentences, and two characters are compared on a both / only-one sort. flagpov (Seeing Someone Else's Point of View, PSHE) and flagnarr (Narrative perspective and unreliable narrators, ages 14+) do not sort narration by pronoun or locate responses in text; flagbkcmp compares whole books. lab_distinct passed under 30% against every flagship lab.

lab_teaches.evidence: Learners discover the rules from feedback: tapping 'the third pig' for 'I huffed and I puffed' asks whether the third pig would say these words; putting '"I am lost," said the little duck' in the character box returns 'The I is inside the speech marks, so a character is talking. The teller says "said" or "whispered": an outside teller'; matching 'Hooray! Puddles!' to Cat returns 'Duck loves water, so it fits them. Cat hates wet fur, so they would feel differently.' Done screens state each rule.

predictions.evidence: Two predictions each with a tempting wrong answer: 'Jack climbed the beanstalk. Who is telling it?' (Jack is tempting because he is the main character; story 5 shows he/the outside teller), and '"I am lost," said the little duck. Who is telling the story?' (the duck: it says I is tempting; step 2 sorts both speech-mark lines as outside teller).

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six questions; each wrong option carries its own message: 'outside' (the teller says I, so a character tells it), 'thing' (a place or thing cannot tell this story), 'named' (the story says Red Riding Hood, not I), 'speech' (the I is inside speech marks), 'none' (said the bear comes from an outside teller), 'wrong' and 'one' (different wants, different feelings), 'problem' and 'detail' (the response is what Ana did next), 'same' and 'facts' (one built, one trusted the fox; the wolf did not eat the third pig).

readability.evidence: Kid text measured FK grade 2.8 against the family limit of 5.0 with sentences like 'A response is what a character does about a problem.' Adult text measured about grade 7.8 against 10.0. Canvas text is short: every story is one or two sentences and the event banners are a single line ('Event: It starts to rain at the picnic.'). Validators passed.

no_filler.evidence: Every kid paragraph states one rule with an example (teller, speech marks, two views, responses). The adult text gives the standards, the first/third person definitions, how to check a point of view, five named mistakes and what each step does. The content gate found no filler phrases and the explanation is under 12% the same as every other lesson, including Seeing Someone Else's Point of View and Narrative perspective.

mobile.evidence: Checked 360 px Android screenshots in light and dark themes for all six steps: story cards wrap to two lines at 18 px, the three teller cards are 50 px tall and full width, the two and three sorting boxes fit side by side with wrapped labels ('outside teller: he, she, they', 'Gingerbread Man'), and the four response sentences stack at about 58 px each. After the first screenshot the third compare box got its own green colour so it is not confused with 'the pig'. Walkthrough passed on iPhone 13.

accessibility.evidence: Every canvas action has a button: one per possible teller ('the wolf is telling the story'), the two narrator boxes with the line read out in the aria-label, Duck/Cat and Mia/Leo with the line they would say, sentence buttons 1 to 4 whose aria-label reads the sentence, and the three compare boxes. Tapping a box also sorts the card. The canvas aria-label updates after every action, challenge feedback is a role=status live region, and axe (WCAG 2.1 AA) found no violations in either theme on desktop and iPhone 13.
